vignette: The highway curves sharply around the coastline, but Leo never sees the slick patch of oil. The tires lose traction. He remembers the sickening crunch of the guardrail, the sudden silence after the airbags deploy, and then the dark. He was in the passenger seat beside his twenty-three-year-old sister, Aroha. He was the one who dragged her from the wreckage as rain mixed with oil on the asphalt. She survived, but she didn't wake up for eleven days. Leo sat by her hospital bed, watching the ventilator breathe for her, replaying every decision he made in those last ten seconds. He still blames himself for taking the wheel that night. The months that followed blur into a quiet exhaustion. He sleeps in his clothes, propped against the wall in his empty apartment. When he closes his eyes, the smell of antiseptic and wet asphalt pulls him under. He wakes up gasping, his heart hammering against his ribs. He checks the lock on his front door three times before allowing himself to relax. He tells his friends he's fine, but he leaves his phone face-down on the kitchen counter because he can't bear the sound of voices overlapping. He avoids the hospital entirely. The thought of the ICU doors makes his stomach turn. He skips the monthly Pacific community gathering, telling them he has closing shifts, though he's been taking time off work. The guilt sits heavy in his ribs. He goes to the community pharmacy because it keeps him moving, but the work has changed. He used to take pride in the rhythm of his day-counting tablets, verifying dosages, explaining interactions with patients. Now, his hands tremble when he measures out controlled substances. He reads each prescription label twice, sometimes three times, convinced he'll miss a decimal point and someone will die. The pharmacopeia on his shelf feels like a foreign language. He avoids the alcohol section entirely, walking a full aisle wide to keep the bottles out of his sightline. When he stands in the checkout line at the grocery store, he scans the exits, calculating how fast he could move if a car came through the front window. He feels detached from his own body, like he's operating it from a distance. He sits across from me now, shoulders drawn up, eyes fixed on a crack in the ceiling. His breath is shallow. I ask him how he's been sleeping. He doesn't answer immediately. He rolls his thumb over Aroha's old ring, which he keeps in his pocket, though he knows logically it serves no purpose. He tells me he's fine. He's working. He's paying rent. But his voice cracks on the last word. He adjusts his watch, a nervous habit he's developed since the accident. The pharmacy bell above the door jingles, and he flinches, his gaze snapping to the entrance before he forces himself back to me. He exhales slowly, fingers drumming against his knee. He looks at his hands, then at the floor, then at me. "I just want it to stop," he says quietly. "I don't know how to let go of the wheel."
